books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Coxey’s Army photograph, 1894; Coney Island trade card, about 1885–1896

stimulus.text: Image 1: An 1894 photograph shows a column of men marching down a dirt road toward Washington, carrying banners. One banner reads “More Money! Less Misery! Good Roads!” A placard shows a portrait with the words “Death to Interest on Bonds.” The caption reads “Coxey’s Army approaching Washington.” Image 2: A color trade card from about 1885–1896, “Scene at Coney Island,” shows boys in suits digging in the sand on a crowded beach, with a sailboat and a paddle steamer on the water and amusement buildings, a tall tower, and an elephant-shaped hotel behind them.
stimulus.source_note: Image 1: 1894 stereograph, Library of Congress (LC-DIG-stereo-1s09209), public domain; image viewed by the writer (shared pool: u6/original-u6-coxeys-army-approaching-washington.jpg). Image 2: chromolithograph trade card, Lindner, Eddy and Clauss, New York, about 1885-1896, public domain; image viewed by the writer (shared pool: u6/u6-coney-island-scene.jpg).

stem: Taken together, what do the two images best show about the United States in the 1890s?

options.text: Ordinary people entered public life to demand help and enjoy leisure
Americans agreed that the federal government should stay out of the economy
options.misconception: The marchers demanded federal action, so they did not agree government should stay out.

options.text: City life had replaced all rural life
options.misconception: Millions still farmed in the 1890s, so city life had not replaced all rural life.

options.text: Protest and leisure both disappeared during the depression
options.misconception: Both images show protest and leisure alive in the 1890s, so neither disappeared.

rationales.A: One image shows a march on Washington and the other a crowded resort: new public action and new public fun.
rationales.B: The marchers ask the federal government to act, so they do not want it to stay out.
rationales.C: Farming still employed millions in the 1890s, so cities had not replaced the countryside.
rationales.D: The images themselves show protest and leisure happening, not disappearing.
rationales.general:
Put the two pictures side by side.
1. Image 1 shows unemployed men marching to Washington with demands.
2. Image 2 shows well-dressed children playing at a crowded commercial resort.
3. One is protest, the other is leisure, and both are mass and public.
4. Background from the books: the 1890s mixed depression and protest with a growing middle-class world of amusements.
Remember: two pictures from one decade can show two sides of the same change.
